title: The Alaska Town Where Almost Everyone Shares One Building
tags: whittier, alaska, begich towers, odd towns
script: In one Alaska town, almost everyone lives under a single roof. Whittier began as a World War Two Army port. Today, nearly all its residents live in Begich Towers, a fourteen-story building finished in 1957. Inside are a post office, a general store, a church and the police office. Kids can reach school through a tunnel. And the only road into town is a one-lane tunnel shared with trains. It closes at night.

title: Kentucky Officials Must Swear They've Never Dueled
tags: strange laws, kentucky, dueling, constitution
script: In Kentucky, lawmakers, public officers and every lawyer must swear they've never fought a duel. It's in Section 228 of the state constitution, adopted in 1891. The oath says they haven't fought a duel with deadly weapons, sent or accepted a challenge, or even acted as a second. Dueling was once a real problem in Kentucky. Lawmakers have debated dropping the pledge, but it remains. Pistols at dawn are officially off.

title: He Destroyed a Wonder of the World to Get Famous
tags: herostratus, temple of artemis, ancient greece, fame
script: In 356 BC, a man burned down one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, just to become famous. His target was the Temple of Artemis at Ephesus. When caught, he admitted he wanted his name remembered forever. So the city came up with the perfect punishment: they made it illegal to ever say his name. It didn't work. Ancient historians wrote it down anyway. His name was Herostratus. And sorry, Ephesus, I just said it.

title: Henry Hudson Was Set Adrift by His Own Crew
tags: henry hudson, mutiny, explorers, hudson bay
script: The explorer who gave his name to a river and a vast bay was cast adrift by his own crew. In 1610, Henry Hudson sailed the ship Discovery into northern Canada, hunting for a route to Asia. After a long winter in James Bay, the crew turned on him. In June 1611, they mutinied. Hudson, his son John, and several others were set adrift in a small open boat. The Discovery sailed away. They were never seen again.

title: Pluto Hasn't Finished One Orbit Since We Found It
tags: pluto, space, solar system, astronomy
script: Since we discovered Pluto, it still hasn't finished a single trip around the Sun. Clyde Tombaugh spotted it on February 18th, 1930, at Lowell Observatory in Arizona. But Pluto is so far away that one orbit takes about 248 Earth years. It was even reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006, before finishing one lap. Astronomers expect its first full orbit since discovery to wrap up on March 23rd, 2178. Set a very long reminder.

title: The Olympics Once Gave Gold Medals for Art
tags: olympics, art competitions, pierre de coubertin, 1912, sports history
script: From 1912 to 1948, you could win an Olympic medal for painting. The Games held official art competitions in architecture, literature, music, painting, and sculpture, and every entry had to be inspired by sport. One American, Walter Winans, won Olympic gold in both shooting and sculpture. And in 1912, the literature gold went to an 'Ode to Sport' entered under a fake name. The real author? The founder of the modern Olympics.

title: The Australian Town Where People Live Underground
tags: coober pedy, australia, opal, underground homes, odd towns
script: In this Australian desert town, many people go home by going underground. Coober Pedy, in the South Australian outback, is known as the opal capital of the world. Summer days are so hot that residents carve homes called dugouts into the hillsides, where the temperature stays nearly constant. There are underground churches too. The landscape has even played alien worlds in movies. Out here, the coolest address is below ground.

title: The Supreme Court Ruled a Tomato Is a Vegetable
tags: tomato, supreme court, strange decisions, food law
script: In 1893, the U.S. Supreme Court officially ruled that a tomato is a vegetable. It all came down to taxes. An import law placed a duty on vegetables, and a New York produce firm run by the Nix family argued tomatoes were fruit. Botanically, they were right. The Court even admitted it. But Justice Horace Gray wrote that people serve tomatoes with dinner, not as dessert. So legally, the vegetable won.

title: Venice's Ruler Married the Sea Every Year
tags: venice, doge, medieval traditions, italy
script: For centuries, the ruler of Venice got married every single year. To the sea. On Ascension Day, the doge sailed out on a golden ceremonial barge and threw a gold ring into the Adriatic, declaring in Latin: we wed thee, O sea, as a sign of true and perpetual dominion. The tradition began around the year one thousand and continued until the Republic fell in 1797. And it's back. Venice's mayor still reenacts the wedding today.

title: A Genius Physicist Bought a Ticket and Disappeared
tags: ettore majorana, physics, disappearance, italy
script: One of the most brilliant physicists of the 1930s bought a boat ticket and disappeared. Ettore Majorana was just 31. Enrico Fermi compared his genius to Galileo and Newton. In March 1938, he set off on a ship from Palermo to Naples and was never seen again. Before leaving, he had withdrawn his savings. In 2015, Italian prosecutors concluded he was probably living in Venezuela in the late 1950s. Why he left remains a mystery.

title: The Moon Is Slowly Drifting Away From Earth
tags: moon, space, tides, apollo
script: The Moon is slowly drifting away from us. Every year, it moves about 3.8 centimeters farther from Earth. We know this because Apollo astronauts left special mirrors on the lunar surface. Scientists fire lasers at them from Earth and time how long the light takes to bounce back, measuring the distance to within millimeters. The cause is ocean tides, whose gravity tugs the Moon forward and pushes it outward. It's not leaving soon. But it is leaving.

title: The Storm That Chased the British Out of Washington
tags: war of 1812, washington dc, 1814, tornado, white house
script: In 1814, a storm helped drive an invading army out of Washington. During the War of 1812, British troops captured the American capital and set fire to the White House and the Capitol. The next day, the sky turned dark. A violent storm, which many believe included a tornado, tore through the city, tossing cannons and dousing the flames with heavy rain. The British soon left. Their occupation lasted only about twenty-six hours.

title: The Arctic Island Feud Fought With Whisky
tags: hans island, whisky war, canada, greenland, borders
script: For decades, two friendly countries feuded over a rock in the Arctic, using flags and liquor. Hans Island sits between Canada and Greenland. In 1984, a Danish minister planted a flag there, and Danish schnapps was reportedly left too. Canadians answered with their own flag and a bottle of Canadian whisky. The Whisky War ended in 2022, when they agreed to split the island. It now has the world's northernmost land border.

title: Tomatoes Were Once Sold as Medicine Pills
tags: tomatoes, quack medicine, food history, 1800s
script: In the 1830s, tomatoes went from suspicious food to miracle medicine. Physician John Cook Bennett claimed tomatoes could treat diarrhea and indigestion, and urged people to eat them, even as catsup. Soon tomato pills were selling across America, promising cures. Then came the twist. By 1869, doctors were openly criticizing the pills, and later investigations found they contained no tomato at all. A cure without the key ingredient.

title: The Female Pharaoh Who Wore a Fake Beard
tags: hatshepsut, ancient egypt, pharaohs, women in history
script: One of ancient Egypt's pharaohs was a woman who was often shown wearing a beard. Hatshepsut ruled for about twenty years, roughly thirty-five hundred years ago. In official statues, she appears in a king's kilt and headcloth, with the traditional false beard of the pharaohs. That beard was a symbol of kingship, not a disguise. Egyptian kings wore them too. Years after her death, many of her images were chiseled away. But her statues survived, beard and all.

title: A Vice President's Daughter Vanished at Sea
tags: theodosia burr, aaron burr, lost at sea, history mystery
script: The daughter of a former American vice president set sail on New Year's Eve and vanished. Theodosia Burr Alston was Aaron Burr's daughter and the wife of South Carolina's governor. On December 31, 1812, she boarded the schooner Patriot in Georgetown, bound for New York. The ship was never heard from again. Most historians blame a storm off Cape Hatteras. Rumors of pirates swirled for a century. Her father believed the sea took her.

title: Platypuses Glow Under UV Light
tags: platypus, animals, australia, biofluorescence
script: As if the platypus wasn't strange enough, it glows. In 2020, scientists were shining ultraviolet light on museum specimens at Chicago's Field Museum. They were studying flying squirrels. Out of curiosity, they checked a platypus too, and its brown fur lit up a bluish green. This is the mammal that lays eggs and has a duck-like bill. Now add UV-glowing fur. Why it glows is still a mystery. Nature just keeps adding features.

title: The Soviet Gift That Spied on America for 7 Years
tags: great seal bug, the thing, cold war, espionage, leon theremin
script: In 1945, Soviet children gave the American ambassador a beautiful gift. Members of the Young Pioneers presented a hand-carved wooden copy of the Great Seal of the United States. Ambassador Averell Harriman hung it in his study in Moscow. Hidden inside was a listening device with no battery and no wires. It only switched on when the Soviets beamed radio waves at it. It went unnoticed for about seven years. Its inventor also created the theremin.

title: A Lost King Was Found Under a Parking Lot
tags: richard iii, leicester, england, archaeology, lost places
script: For centuries, nobody knew exactly where King Richard the Third was buried. He died at the Battle of Bosworth in 1485. In 2012, researchers compared old maps of Leicester, England, and dug up a city parking lot where a lost friary church once stood. Beneath its choir, they found a skeleton with a curved spine. DNA from living relatives on his sister's family line confirmed it. A king, under the parking spaces.

title: Lincoln Logs Were Invented by Frank Lloyd Wright's Son
tags: lincoln logs, toys, frank lloyd wright, odd origins
script: America's classic log cabin toy was invented by a famous architect's son. Around 1916, John Lloyd Wright was in Tokyo, working with his father, Frank Lloyd Wright, on the Imperial Hotel. The building's interlocking timber construction gave him an idea. He created notched toy logs that kids could stack into cabins. He named them after Abraham Lincoln, who was born in a log cabin. Big architecture, tiny logs.

title: Athens Exiled a Man for Being Too Fair
tags: ancient athens, ostracism, aristides, democracy
script: In ancient Athens, you could be voted out of the city for being too good. Once a year, citizens could scratch a name on a piece of broken pottery, and the top name was exiled for ten years. According to Plutarch, a voter who couldn't write asked a stranger to scratch the name Aristides. Why? He was tired of hearing him called the Just. The stranger wrote it down. The stranger was Aristides himself.

title: Elgar's Secret Note Has Stumped Everyone Since 1897
tags: dorabella cipher, edward elgar, codes, unsolved
script: In 1897, the composer Edward Elgar sent a friend a coded note that no one has ever cracked. Tucked into a letter to Dora Penny were 87 tiny symbols made of looping semicircles, in three lines. Elgar loved puzzles. Dora never solved it, though he later honored her as Dorabella in his Enigma Variations. Experts have proposed answers for decades. A 2007 Elgar Society contest found no winner. Maybe it's a message. Maybe a joke.

title: Germany Finished Paying for WWI in 2010
tags: world war one, reparations, germany, 2010, treaty of versailles
script: World War One ended in 1918, but Germany didn't finish paying for it until 2010. After the war, Germany was ordered to pay enormous reparations. Payments stalled again and again. Hitler stopped them entirely. In 1953, a deal cut the remaining loan debt in half and postponed part of it until Germany reunified. So on October 3, 2010, the twentieth anniversary of reunification, Germany made its final payment: about ninety-four million dollars.

title: Tulip Mania Wasn't as Crazy as You Think
tags: tulip mania, dutch golden age, economic bubbles, myths
script: In 1637, a single tulip bulb reportedly sold for more than a fancy house in Amsterdam. That's tulip mania, history's most famous bubble. Prices for rare bulbs soared, then crashed in February 1637. Legend says fortunes were wiped out. But historian Anne Goldgar searched the records and said she couldn't find anybody who went bankrupt. The wild tales came largely from moral pamphlets and an 1841 book. The bubble was real. The panic was exaggerated.

title: The Statue of Liberty Used to Be a Lighthouse
tags: statue of liberty, lighthouse, new york, 1886, landmarks
script: For about fifteen years, the Statue of Liberty was officially a lighthouse. When it was dedicated in 1886, the federal Lighthouse Board took charge, and its torch was supposed to guide ships into New York Harbor. One newspaper said it looked more like a glowworm than a beacon. Officials eventually judged it useless for navigation, and in 1902 the light was switched off. Back then, she wasn't even green. She was shiny copper brown.
